text: AK - Actinic Keratosis | BKL - Benign Keratosis-like Lesion | DF - Dermatofibroma | VASC - Vascular Lesion ========================================================================================================== Source: Adapted from AAD dermatology guidelines (educational summary) === AK: ACTINIC KERATOSIS === OVERVIEW Actinic keratosis (AK) is a pre-malignant lesion caused by cumulative UV damage. It is the precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Treatment is recommended to prevent malignant transformation. CLINICAL FEATURES - Rough, scaly patch on sun-damaged skin - Flat to slightly raised patch with dry, scaly surface - Itching, burning, or tenderness in the affected area - Hard, wart-like surface; color varies (pink, red, or brown) - Commonly on face, lips, ears, back of hands, forearms, scalp, neck MANAGEMENT - Cryotherapy: liquid nitrogen — most common treatment - Topical agents: 5-FU, imiquimod, ingenol mebutate for field treatment - Photodynamic therapy: for multiple/field AKs - All AKs should be treated — 10% may progress to SCC within 10 years - Annual skin checks recommended after diagnosis PATIENT ADVICE - Strict UV avoidance and SPF 50+ daily - Monitor and consult a doctor if the lesion changes, grows, bleeds, or becomes painful === BKL: BENIGN KERATOSIS-LIKE LESION (Seborrhoeic Keratosis) === OVERVIEW Seborrhoeic keratoses are benign, non-cancerous growths that become more common with age. They are entirely benign but can be mistaken for melanoma or BCC. CLINICAL FEATURES - "Stuck-on" appearance — waxy, warty surface - Range from light tan to dark brown or black - Varies in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres - Multiple lesions common; found on trunk, face, shoulders, back - NOT caused by sun exposure; NOT pre-malignant MANAGEMENT - No treatment required if benign - Removal for cosmetic reasons or if inflamed/irritated (cryotherapy, curettage) - Biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain (cannot reliably exclude melanoma clinically) PATIENT ADVICE - Lesions are benign — no cancer risk - Monitor and consult a doctor if any individual lesion changes rapidly, bleeds, or becomes asymmetric — these may indicate a co-existing melanoma === DF: DERMATOFIBROMA === OVERVIEW Dermatofibromas are benign fibrous nodules, most commonly found on the legs. They are harmless and require no treatment unless symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome. CLINICAL FEATURES - Firm, raised bump, usually 0.5–1.5cm - Typically pink, red, grey, or brown - "Dimple sign": pinching the lesion causes it to dimple inward - Slightly tender to touch; may itch MANAGEMENT - No treatment required - Surgical excision if cosmetically bothersome or symptomatic - Biopsy if diagnosis uncertain (rare malignant variants: dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans) PATIENT ADVICE - Lesion is benign; monitoring sufficient - Monitor and consult a doctor if it changes, grows rapidly, or becomes painful === VASC: VASCULAR LESION === OVERVIEW Vascular lesions include a heterogeneous group: haemangiomas, pyogenic granulomas, angiokeratomas, cherry angiomas. Most are benign but pyogenic granuloma bleeds readily and may mimic amelanotic melanoma. CLINICAL FEATURES - Pyogenic granuloma: rapidly growing, friable, bleeds easily — RED FLAG for referral - Cherry angioma: small, bright-red dome; extremely common; entirely benign - Angiokeratoma: dark red/purple warty papule; may mimic melanoma MANAGEMENT - Cherry

Most are benign but pyogenic granuloma bleeds readily and may mimic amelanotic melanoma. CLINICAL FEATURES - Pyogenic granuloma: rapidly growing, friable, bleeds easily — RED FLAG for referral - Cherry angioma: small, bright-red dome; extremely common; entirely benign - Angiokeratoma: dark red/purple warty papule; may mimic melanoma MANAGEMENT - Cherry angioma: no treatment required - Pyogenic granuloma: excision or shave biopsy — always send for histology - Any bleeding vascular lesion should be evaluated to exclude amelanotic melanoma PATIENT ADVICE - Monitor and consult a doctor if the lesion bleeds, grows rapidly, or changes - Bleeding lesions require prompt evaluation regardless of apparent cause DISCLAIMER (ALL CLASSES) This information is for decision support only. No AI output should be interpreted as a definitive diagnosis. A qualified dermatologist must evaluate all lesions. Never state "you are fine" or "no cancer" based on AI screening alone.

BCC - Basal Cell Carcinoma Clinical Guidelines =============================================== Source: Adapted from AAD/NICE dermatology guidelines (educational summary) OVERVIEW Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer worldwide, arising from basal cells of the epidermis. It grows slowly and rarely metastasises, but causes significant local tissue destruction if left untreated. Early treatment is curative. CLINICAL FEATURES - Pearly or waxy bump, often with visible blood vessels (telangiectasia) - Flat, flesh-coloured or brown scar-like lesion - Bleeding or scabbing sore that heals and returns - Pink growth with raised edges and a crusted centre - Commonly on sun-exposed areas: face, ears, neck, scalp, shoulders RISK FACTORS - Cumulative UV exposure (sun, tanning beds) - Fair skin, light eyes/hair, freckles - Personal or family history of BCC or other skin cancers - Immunosuppression (organ transplant recipients have 65x higher risk) - Radiation therapy history MANAGEMENT - Surgical excision: primary treatment; high cure rates (>95%) - Mohs micrographic surgery: for high-risk or recurrent BCC - Topical treatments (imiquimod, 5-FU): for superficial BCC only - Photodynamic therapy: for superficial BCC in cosmetically sensitive areas - Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib): for advanced/metastatic BCC MONITORING AND FOLLOW-UP - Annual skin checks after first BCC — 50% risk of second BCC within 5 years - Full-body skin examination by dermatologist - Patient self-examination monthly PATIENT ADVICE - Strict sun protection (SPF 50+, protective clothing, avoid peak UV hours) - Report any new growths, sores that don't heal, or lesion changes promptly - Monitor and consult a doctor if the lesion changes in any way DISCLAIMER This is decision-support information only. A qualified dermatologist must confirm any diagnosis. AI output should never state "no cancer" or "you are fine." DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS BCC vs: SCC (squamous cell — grows faster, higher metastasis risk), MEL (melanoma), BKL (seborrhoeic keratosis — benign), VASC (vascular lesion), AK (actinic keratosis).

MEL - Melanoma Clinical Guidelines ==================================== Source: Adapted from AAD/WHO dermatology guidelines (educational summary) OVERVIEW Melanoma is the most dangerous form of skin cancer, arising from melanocytes. Early detection is critical — 5-year survival exceeds 98% if caught at stage I, but drops to ~25% at stage IV. ABCDE RULE FOR DETECTION - Asymmetry: One half unlike the other - Border: Ragged, notched, or blurred edges - Color: Variation in color (tan, brown, black, red, white, or blue) - Diameter: Larger than 6mm (pencil eraser size) - Evolving: Any change in size, shape, color, or new symptom (bleeding, itching) RED FLAGS REQUIRING URGENT REFERRAL - Rapidly growing lesion (weeks, not months) - Spontaneous bleeding or ulceration - Irregular or notched border - Itching AND pain simultaneously present - Lesion diameter > 6mm with color variation CLINICAL MANAGEMENT - Urgent dermatology referral within 2 weeks (suspected melanoma pathway) - Dermoscopy evaluation by trained clinician - Excision biopsy is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis - Sentinel lymph node biopsy for lesions > 1mm Breslow thickness - Do NOT apply topical treatments before biopsy — it alters histology PATIENT ADVICE - Avoid sun exposure; use SPF 50+ sunscreen daily - Perform monthly self-skin checks - Monitor lesion for ANY change in size, shape, colour, or symptoms - Do not delay seeking evaluation if the lesion changes DISCLAIMER This is decision-support information only. A qualified dermatologist must confirm any diagnosis. Do not tell patients they are cancer-free based on AI output alone. Always use: "Monitor and consult a doctor if it changes." DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS MEL must be distinguished from: NV (benign nevus), BKL (seborrhoeic keratosis), BCC (basal cell carcinoma — also malignant but rarely metastasises), DF (dermatofibroma).

NV - Melanocytic Nevus (Common Mole) Clinical Guidelines ========================================================= Source: Adapted from AAD dermatology guidelines (educational summary) OVERVIEW Melanocytic nevi (common moles) are benign proliferations of melanocytes. They are extremely common — most adults have 10–40 moles. The vast majority are entirely benign, but any changing mole warrants clinical evaluation. CLINICAL FEATURES (BENIGN CHARACTERISTICS) - Symmetric shape (both halves match) - Smooth, well-defined border - Uniform single color (tan, brown, or flesh-toned) - Diameter usually < 6mm - Stable over years — NOT evolving WHEN A NEVUS MAY BECOME CONCERNING - Asymmetry develops - Border becomes irregular, notched, or blurred - Color changes or becomes variegated (multiple colors) - Diameter increases beyond 6mm - Evolving: any change in size, shape, color, or new symptoms (bleeding, itching, pain) - A new mole appearing after age 50 TYPES OF NEVI - Common acquired nevus: most prevalent; develops in childhood/adolescence - Congenital nevus: present at birth; large ones have slightly higher MEL risk - Dysplastic (atypical) nevus: irregular features; marker of elevated MEL risk - Blue nevus: blue-grey color; benign but can mimic melanoma MANAGEMENT - Most benign nevi require no treatment - Excision biopsy if: changing, symptomatic, cosmetically bothersome, or diagnostic doubt - Dysplastic nevi: excise if severely atypical; regular surveillance otherwise - High nevus count (>50) is a melanoma risk factor — annual skin checks recommended PATIENT ADVICE - Perform monthly self-examination - Photograph baseline moles and compare at 3-month intervals - Any change in a mole should prompt dermatology evaluation - Monitor and consult a doctor if it changes - Use SPF 50+ sunscreen — UV exposure promotes nevus evolution DISCLAIMER This AI tool provides decision support only. A dermatologist must evaluate any changing or symptomatic mole. Do not interpret "NV" prediction as confirmation that no further evaluation is needed. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS NV vs: MEL (melanoma — must rule out with ABCDE), BKL (seborrhoeic keratosis — stuck-on appearance), DF (dermatofibroma — firm, dimples with pinch).

SCC - Squamous Cell Carcinoma Clinical Guidelines ================================================== Source: Adapted from AAD/NICE dermatology guidelines (educational summary) OVERVIEW Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common skin cancer, arising from squamous cells of the epidermis. Unlike BCC, SCC has a meaningful metastasis risk (~2-5% overall; higher in immunocompromised patients or high-risk sites like lips/ears). CLINICAL FEATURES - Firm red nodule or flat lesion with scaly, crusted surface - New sore or raised area on an old scar - Rough, scaly patch on the lip - Red sore or rough patch inside the mouth - Wart-like growth - Commonly on sun-exposed areas; also mucous membranes and genitals RED FLAGS FOR SCC - Rapid growth over weeks - Ulceration or spontaneous bleeding - Perineural invasion (numbness, tingling around lesion) - Lesion on lip, ear, or in immunocompromised patient - Regional lymph node enlargement RELATIONSHIP TO ACTINIC KERATOSIS (AK) - AK is the precursor lesion to SCC - ~10% of untreated AKs may progress to SCC over 10 years - AK management reduces SCC incidence MANAGEMENT - Surgical excision: standard treatment with clear margins - Mohs surgery: for high-risk SCC (face, recurrent, large, perineural) - Radiation therapy: for inoperable cases or post-excision adjuvant - Sentinel node biopsy: for high-risk SCC (>2cm, >2mm depth, immunocompromised) - Cemiplimab / pembrolizumab: immunotherapy for advanced/metastatic SCC PATIENT ADVICE - Immediate dermatology referral for any suspected SCC - Sun protection: SPF 50+, protective clothing year-round - Stop smoking (risk factor for oral/lip SCC) - Monitor and consult a doctor if the lesion changes in size, colour, or texture DISCLAIMER This is decision-support information only. A dermatologist must confirm diagnosis. Never tell a patient they are cancer-free based on AI screening output alone. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS SCC vs: AK (precursor — treatment prevents progression), BCC (slower, no metastasis), MEL (melanoma — higher systemic risk), VASC (vascular lesion — different management).
